Methadone is available in various formulations, including oral tablets (10 mg, 40 mg as hydrochloride), oral liquids (1 mg/mL, 2 mg/mL, 5 mg/mL as hydrochloride), and oral concentrates (10 mg/mL as hydrochloride). Due to its complex pharmacokinetics and significant inter-individual variability, methadone should only be initiated by practitioners experienced in its use. Dose titration must be conducted with close clinical monitoring over several days. Methadone is indicated for moderate-to-severe persistent pain. Contraindications include hypersensitivity to opioid agonists or any component of the formulation, acute respiratory depression, acute asthma, paralytic ileus, concurrent or recent (within 14 days) use of monoamine oxidase inhibitors, uncontrolled raised intracranial pressure or head injury, and coma. Precautions include impaired respiratory function, avoiding rapid injection (to prevent chest wall rigidity and ventilation difficulty), history of cardiac conduction abnormalities, family history of sudden death (ECG monitoring recommended), QT interval prolongation, asthma, hypotension, shock, obstructive or inflammatory bowel disorders, biliary tract disease, convulsive disorders, hypothyroidism, adrenocortical insufficiency, diabetes mellitus, impaired consciousness, acute pancreatitis, myasthenia gravis, hepatic or renal impairment, and toxic psychosis. Abrupt withdrawal after prolonged treatment should be avoided. Methadone is generally reserved for patients who do not respond well to morphine or other strong opioids. In cases of severe renal impairment (GFR <10 mL/min or serum creatinine >700 micromol/L), the dose should be reduced by 50% and titrated based on response. Methadone elimination primarily occurs via the liver, so significant accumulation in renal failure is unlikely. In hepatic impairment, methadone should be avoided or the dose reduced, as it may precipitate coma. Common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, constipation, dry mouth, biliary spasm, respiratory depression, drowsiness, muscle rigidity, hypotension, bradycardia, tachycardia, palpitations, edema, postural hypotension, hallucinations, vertigo, euphoria, dysphoria, dependence, confusion, urinary retention, and ureteric spasm. Less common effects include restlessness, dyspnea, hypoventilation, depersonalization, dysarthria, amnesia, incoordination, paresthesia, malaise, agitation, tremor, muscle weakness, hypertension, dizziness, itching, bronchospasm, dysmenorrhea, dry eyes, and hyperprolactinemia. Rare effects include QT interval prolongation, torsades de pointes, hypothermia, circulatory depression, cardiac arrest, hiccups, arrhythmia, paralytic ileus, hemoptysis, psychosis, seizures, shock, asystole, pyrexia, ataxia, muscle fasciculation, and raised intracranial pressure. Methadone interacts with various medications, including abacavir (reduced plasma concentration of methadone), amiodarone (increased risk of QT prolongation), atomoxetine (increased risk of ventricular arrhythmias), carbamazepine (reduced methadone plasma concentration), CNS depressants (additive or potentiating effects), efavirenz (reduced methadone plasma concentration), fluvoxamine (possibly increased methadone plasma concentration), fosamprenavir (reduced methadone plasma concentration), medicines that prolong the QT interval (increased risk of QT prolongation), monoamine oxidase inhibitors (severe and unpredictable potentiation of opioids), naloxone and naltrexone (precipitation of opioid withdrawal symptoms), nelfinavir (reduced methadone plasma concentration), nevirapine (possibly reduced methadone plasma concentration), opioid antagonists/partial agonists (may precipitate withdrawal symptoms), phenobarbital (reduced methadone plasma concentration), phenytoin (accelerated methadone metabolism, reduced effect, and risk of withdrawal symptoms), quinine (increased risk of QT prolongation), rifampicin (accelerated methadone metabolism), ritonavir (reduced methadone plasma concentration), voriconazole (increased methadone plasma concentration), and zidovudine (possibly increased zidovudine concentration). 2. Morphine is available in various formulations, including injection (10 mg/mL as morphine hydrochloride or sulfate), oral liquid (10 mg/5 mL as morphine hydrochloride or sulfate), immediate-release tablets (10 mg as morphine sulfate), and prolonged-release tablets (10 mg, 30 mg, 60 mg as morphine sulfate). Morphine is subject to international control under the Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs, 1961. It is used for moderate-to-severe pain (acute and chronic), myocardial infarction, acute pulmonary edema, and as an adjunct during major surgery and postoperative analgesia. Contraindications include acute respiratory depression, acute alcoholism, risk of paralytic ileus, raised intracranial pressure or head injury (as it affects pupillary responses vital for neurological assessment), and injection in pheochromocytoma. Precautions include renal and hepatic impairment, reduced dose or avoidance in older and debilitated patients, hypothyroidism, convulsive disorders, decreased respiratory reserve, acute asthma, hypotension, prostatic hypertrophy, pregnancy, and breastfeeding. Abrupt withdrawal can lead to severe withdrawal symptoms. For acute pain, morphine can be administered subcutaneously (not suitable for edematous patients), intramuscularly, or intravenously at 2–10 mg every 4 hours as needed. For chronic pain, it can be given orally (immediate-release tablets) or subcutaneously/intravenously at 2–20 mg every 4 hours, with dose adjustments based on need. Oral doses should be approximately double the corresponding injected dose. For myocardial infarction, slow intravenous injection (2 mg/min) is given at 5–10 mg, with a further 5–10 mg if necessary. For acute pulmonary edema, slow intravenous injection (2 mg/min) is given at 5–10 mg. Sustained-release capsules for once-daily administration are also available. Sustained-release tablets should be taken at regular intervals and not on an as-needed basis for episodic or breakthrough pain. They should not be crushed. Common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting (especially initially), constipation, drowsiness, dry mouth, anorexia, spasm of urinary and biliary tracts, bradycardia, tachycardia, palpitations, euphoria, decreased libido, rash, urticaria, pruritus, sweating, headache, facial flushing, vertigo, postural hypotension, hypothermia, hallucinations, confusion, dependence, and miosis. Larger doses can cause respiratory depression, hypotension, and muscle rigidity. 3. Naloxone is available as an injection (0.4 mg/mL as hydrochloride in 1 mL ampoule) and is indicated for opioid overdose. There are no contraindications for its use in treating severe or life-threatening opioid toxicity, such as respiratory depression. Precautions include cautious dosing to avoid severe withdrawal syndrome after prolonged opioid administration and in opioid-tolerant patients, cardiovascular disease, and postoperative patients (as it may reverse analgesia and increase blood pressure). In cases of renal impairment, excretion of some opioids and/or their active metabolites (e.g., codeine, dextropropoxyphene, dihydrocodeine, morphine, pethidine, oxycodone) is delayed, leading to accumulation. Extended treatment with naloxone infusion may be required to reverse opioid effects. No dose adjustment is necessary for hepatic impairment. Common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, and sweating. Less common effects include tachycardia and ventricular arrhythmias. Rare effects include cardiac arrest. There are no known interactions where concomitant use of naloxone with other medicines should be avoided. 4. Oxycodone is available in various formulations, including tablets (5 mg, 10 mg, 15 mg, 20 mg, 30 mg as hydrochloride), modified-release tablets (5 mg, 10 mg, 15 mg, 20 mg, 30 mg, 40 mg, 60 mg, 80 mg, 160 mg as hydrochloride), capsules (5 mg, 10 mg, 20 mg as hydrochloride), oral liquid (1 mg/mL as hydrochloride), and concentrated oral liquid (10 mg/mL, 20 mg/mL as hydrochloride). It is indicated for moderate-to-severe persistent pain. Contraindications include hypersensitivity to opioid agonists or any component of the formulation, acute respiratory depression, acute asthma, paralytic ileus, concurrent or recent (within 14 days) use of monoamine oxidase inhibitors, uncontrolled raised intracranial pressure or head injury, and coma. Precautions include impaired respiratory function, avoiding rapid injection (to prevent chest wall rigidity and ventilation difficulty), bradycardia, asthma, hypotension, shock, obstructive or inflammatory bowel disorders, biliary tract disease, convulsive disorders, hypothyroidism, adrenocortical insufficiency, diabetes mellitus, impaired consciousness, acute pancreatitis, myasthenia gravis, hepatic or renal impairment, and toxic psychosis. Abrupt withdrawal after prolonged treatment should be avoided. For renal impairment, dose reduction may be required, starting with the lowest dose and titrating based on response. In moderate-to-severe hepatic impairment, the dose should be reduced by 50% or avoided. Common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, constipation, diarrhea, dry mouth, sedation, biliary spasm, abdominal pain, anorexia, dyspepsia, pruritus, somnolence, and dizziness. Less common effects include muscle rigidity, hypotension, respiratory depression, bronchospasm, dyspnea, impaired cough reflex, asthenia, anxiety, chills, muscle fasciculation, postural hypotension, hallucinations, vertigo, euphoria, dysphoria, dizziness, confusion, bradycardia, tachycardia, palpitations, edema, mood changes, dependence, drowsiness, sleep disturbances, headache, miosis, visual disturbances, sweating, flushing, rash, urticaria, restlessness, difficulty with micturition, urinary retention, ureteric spasm, gastritis, flatulence, dysphagia, taste disturbance, belching, hiccups, vasodilation, supraventricular tachycardia, syncope, amnesia, hypoesthesia, pyrexia, amenorrhea, hypotonia, paresthesia, disorientation, malaise, agitation, speech disorder, tremor, and dry skin. Rare effects include raised intracranial pressure, circulatory depression, cardiac arrest, respiratory arrest, shock, paralytic ileus, and seizures. Oxycodone interacts with CNS depressants (additive or potentiating effects), monoamine oxidase inhibitors (severe and unpredictable potentiation of opioids), naloxone and naltrexone (precipitation of opioid withdrawal symptoms), and opioid antagonists/partial agonists (may precipitate withdrawal symptoms). 5. Paracetamol is available in various formulations, including oral liquid (120 mg/5 mL), suppository (100 mg), tablet (100–500 mg), and injection for IV infusion (10 mg/mL). It is used for mild-to-moderate pain, including dysmenorrhea, headache, pain relief in osteoarthritis and soft tissue lesions, pyrexia (including post-immunization pyrexia), and acute migraine attacks. Precautions include hepatic impairment, renal impairment, alcohol dependence, and breastfeeding. Unintentional overdose of paracetamol can result in hepatotoxicity and death. To reduce this risk, the dose should not exceed the maximum recommended dose, should be appropriate for the patient’s weight, and should be reduced when risk factors for hepatotoxicity exist. The typical dose is 500 mg to 1 g every 4–6 hours, with a maximum of 4 g daily. IV paracetamol can be used when oral or rectal administration is not possible. The dose depends on body weight and the presence/absence of risk factors for hepatotoxicity. For patients >50 kg, the dose is 1 g up to every 4 hours, with a maximum of 4 g/24 hours. For patients >50 kg with risk factors, the maximum dose is restricted to 3 g/24 hours. For patients 10–50 kg, the dose is 15 mg/kg up to every 4 hours, with a maximum of 60 mg/kg/24 hours. For patients with severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance <30 mL/min), the minimum interval must be ≥6 hours. Rare adverse effects include rash and blood disorders. Liver damage (and less frequently renal damage) can occur following overdose.
